Workshop 2 · Sessions 4–6 · Thursday 8 October 2026

From words to search: tokens, terms and the inverted index

Search for "leak" in 30,000 reviews and you miss "Leaking" and "leaked", but you do find "no leaks at all". Today we turn raw text into clean index terms, then build the data structure behind every search box, the inverted index, and answer Boolean queries over all 30,000 reviews in milliseconds.

Open slides Notebooks and data Practice problems

By the end of this workshop you can

  • split text into tokens, and count tokens and types
  • normalise tokens with case folding, stop-word removal, stemming and lemmatisation, and say what each one gains and loses
  • build a term–document incidence matrix and an inverted index by hand and in Python
  • answer AND, OR and NOT queries by merging postings lists, and order the terms to do less work
  • explain how normalisation trades precision against recall in search, and why Boolean search has no ranking

Course outcome CO1 · Reading: [SLP] Chapter 2 · [IIR] Chapters 1 and 2.2

2. Why search, why managers?

Every organisation you will work in runs on search: the search box on an e-commerce site, a support team's knowledge base, a legal team hunting through contracts, an analyst pulling "every complaint about the new model" out of a ticket system. When search fails, it fails quietly. A shopper who types "refrigerator filter" and gets no results doesn't complain; they leave.

You probably won't write a search engine at work, but you may well buy, configure or judge one, and the settings come down to choices you will learn today. Should "leaking" find "leaked"? Should "fridge" find "refrigerator"? Should "no leaks" count as a leak? Each choice trades finding more against finding junk, the same precision–recall trade-off as Workshop 1.

3. Tokens, terms and the inverted index in five minutes

Tokens and types. Before a computer can search for words, it has to decide what a word is. Tokenisation cuts text into tokens: "The filter leaks. The jug doesn't." might become the · filter · leaks · the · jug · doesn't, which is 6 tokens. The distinct ones are called types, here 5, because the appears twice. The set of all types is the vocabulary.

Normalisation maps different tokens to the same term, so a search finds them all:

Step Example Gains Risks
Case folding Filter → filter Filter finds filter US (the country) becomes us
Stop-word removal drop the, a, of, not a smaller index not leaking becomes leaking
Stemming (rules) leaks, leaking, leaked → leak one search finds all three generic, general → gener
Lemmatisation (dictionary) ran → run, mice → mouse real words needs the part of speech; slower

The inverted index. A book's index lists, for each important word, the pages where it appears. A search engine does the same for every term: the term, then the sorted list of document IDs that contain it, called its postings list.

filter  →  1, 2
ice     →  3
leak    →  1, 2, 3

To answer filter AND leak, walk along both lists at once and keep the IDs that appear in both: here 1 and 2. Because the lists are sorted, the walk never goes back, so it takes at most as many steps as the two lists have IDs between them. That is why a search over billions of pages takes a fraction of a second.

4. Read

The examples are Shakespeare plays rather than reviews, but the ideas are identical.
  • [SLP] Jurafsky & Martin, Chapter 2, Words and Tokens: the sections on words, morphemes and corpora, and on rule-based tokenisation. Skim byte-pair encoding; it returns in Workshop 9.

Handout: search cheat sheet

Print this page, or keep it open during the labs.

Words

token one occurrence of a word in the text
type a distinct token
vocabulary the set of types
term a normalised type: what the index stores
stem what is left after a stemmer cuts off endings: replac
lemma the dictionary form: ran → run
stop word a very frequent word: the, of, not

Index

incidence matrix terms × documents, 1 if present
inverted index term → sorted doc IDs
postings list the doc IDs for one term
document frequency the length of a term's postings list
sparse almost all zeros
positional index term → doc ID → positions

Boolean queries

a AND b in both lists
a OR b in either list
a AND NOT b in a's list, not b's
order of ANDs shortest list first
"ice maker" phrase: needs positions

The AND merge

intersect(p1, p2):
    answer = []; i = j = 0
    while i < len(p1) and j < len(p2):
        if p1[i] == p2[j]:  answer.append(p1[i]); i += 1; j += 1
        elif p1[i] < p2[j]: i += 1
        else:               j += 1
    return answer

At most len(p1) + len(p2) comparisons. OR keeps every ID it passes (and the leftovers of both lists); AND NOT keeps an ID from p1 only when p2 has passed it without a match (and the leftovers of p1).

Python and NLTK

re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+(?:'[a-z]+)?", text.lower()) tokenise for search
nltk.word_tokenize(text) NLTK's tokeniser: splits n't, keeps 24.99
set(stopwords.words("english")) 198 English stop words (includes no, not)
PorterStemmer().stem("leaking") 'leak'
WordNetLemmatizer().lemmatize("ran", pos="v") 'run'
index.setdefault(term, []).append(doc_id) build an inverted index
sorted(lists, key=len) shortest postings list first

Normalisation and search quality

More normalisation (stemming, case folding, synonyms) Less normalisation (exact tokens)
finds more forms of the word: recall ↑ misses leaking when you search leak: recall ↓
also finds generally for generic: precision ↓ what you find is what you typed: precision ↑
smaller index larger index
